output:
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, maid and cook, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Madame Häfeli. You are not in trouble. I want the evening in order, one thing at a time. Begin with the dinner.

ROSA: I served the dinner, Herr Inspektor, and then I cleared it. Madame wants the champagne glasses set out in rows on the tray, and I set them out.

MATTHEY: Tell me about your kitchen clock.

ROSA: It is on the wall above the stove. It is a cheap American alarm clock, very loud. I keep it fast on purpose. If the clock says a thing is late, then I am already late, and so nothing in my kitchen is ever late. Monsieur used to laugh at me for it.

MATTHEY: When the temple struck ten, what did your kitchen clock show?

ROSA: A quarter past ten by my kitchen clock. I remember because I was looking at the glasses and thinking they were not all dry.

MATTHEY: Did anyone come down to the kitchen that evening?

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at twenty-three minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven. She is a quiet girl. She does not talk when she is thinking, but she is a good girl.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything from the upper floors?

ROSA: We heard Madame's piano begin at twelve minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and stop at one minute past eleven by my kitchen clock. It was Chopin. Madame always plays Chopin when she is sad, or when she wants people to think she is not sad.

MATTHEY: Did you hear the hall clock?

ROSA: I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed three minutes past eleven. You know the old clock in the hall, with the face. It strikes its hours from its own face, and everybody in this house knows it.

MATTHEY: After the hall clock struck eleven, what did you do?

ROSA: I finished the last of the glasses. Then the toast was to be drunk, and the master had not come down. So I went up the stairs to fetch him for the toast.

MATTHEY: What did you find?

ROSA: The master was on the floor of the atelier, by his bench. He was not moving. His watch was in his hand. I saw the mallet on the boards, and I will not say more about that, Herr Inspektor. I cannot.

MATTHEY: Do you know what time you went up?

ROSA: I did not look at any clock. I was thinking about the glasses and about Madame. I did not think of the time until I was on the stairs.

MATTHEY: Have you anything else to tell me?

ROSA: Only that I have been in this house a long time, and Madame has always been good to me. I want to help her. I am frightened of the police. I was frightened of you when you came in. But I have told you what I know, and I have told you the truth. Herrgott, I have told you the truth.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Madame Häfeli. Please do not leave the house until I say so. Send Mademoiselle Ruedi in to me.
